text: Real questions rarely involve just two columns. Who churns depends on tenure, region, channel, and more, all at once. Multivariate exploration means looking at three or more variables together, usually by adding a third dimension to a chart you already know: color, facets, or a second grouping key.

Take the tenure-versus-orders scatter from last lesson and color each point by whether that customer churned. The churned points cluster toward the left, at low tenure. That's a three-variable story you couldn't see in the two-variable scatter alone.

A pivot table reshapes data into a grid: one category on rows, one on columns, an aggregate in the cells. Churn rate by region and channel: South is darkest across all three channels, consistent with the last lesson. The highest cell, South and app, hits thirty-five percent.

Always check the cell sizes behind a colorful rate. Swapping to a count shows South and app has only twenty customers, and West and app has nineteen. A rate from twenty people can swing a lot. A dark cell with a small count is a lead, not a finding.

Instead of color, split a chart into small multiples with relplot, one panel per channel, so you can check whether a pattern holds everywhere. For a broad survey of many numeric columns at once, use a pair plot, every pair as a scatter, every column as a distribution on the diagonal.

Tables do multivariate work too. Cut tenure into bands and compare churn: zero to twelve months, twenty-nine point five percent, over a hundred thirty-nine customers. Thirteen to twenty-four months, twenty-three point five percent. Twenty-five plus months, just eleven point eight percent. Churn drops steadily as tenure grows.

Watch for confounders: a third variable driving both things you're comparing. If South's customers were simply newer on average, its high churn might be a tenure effect, not a region effect. Break the data down by that third variable and see whether the pattern survives. Next: correlation analysis.
